abstract: ABSTRACT Radiation‐induced heart disease (RIHD) has garnered increasing clinical attention. While oxidative stress plays a pivotal role in RIHD pathogenesis and progression, the involvement of ferroptosis—a regulated cell death pathway closely linked to oxidative stress‐remains poorly characterized. Danhong injection (DHI), a clinically approved traditional Chinese medicine, is widely used for treating cardiovascular disorders because of its anti‐inflammatory and antioxidant properties. Therefore, we investigated whether DHI exerts therapeutic effects against RIHD by suppressing ferroptosis. We established both in vivo and in vitro RIHD models. Ferrostatin‐1 (Fer‐1), a selective ferroptosis inhibitor, was used as a positive control. Mice and cardiomyocytes (H9C2 and AC16 cell lines) were treated with DHI postirradiation. Myocardial tissue/cellular/mitochondrial damage was comprehensively assessed through histopathological and functional analyses. Oxidative/antioxidant imbalance was quantified via biochemical assays, and ferroptosis‐related protein expression was evaluated using immunohistochemistry and Western blotting. Finally, transcriptomic and metabolomic sequencing, coupled with bioinformatics approaches, was performed using murine myocardial tissues to elucidate molecular alterations. X‐irradiation induced structural and functional damage in myocardial tissues and cells, accompanied by oxidative stress and ferroptosis activation. DHI treatment significantly mitigated those effects, restoring myocardial integrity and viability. Differentially expressed genes and metabolites were predominantly enriched in immune response pathways and metabolic reprogramming processes. Promising RNA–metabolite interactions that may serve as therapeutic targets for future investigations were revealed. DHI ameliorates RIHD by inhibiting ferroptosis. Integrated multiomics not only validated the therapeutic potential of DHI but also provided novel insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying radiation‐induced cardiac injury.

Materials and Methods
2.1
Animal Models and Irradiation Protocol
Male C57BL/6 mice (6–8 weeks old,
N
= 80, purchased from the Animal Experiment Center of Lanzhou Veterinary Research Institute) were housed under standard conditions with ad libitum access to food and water. After one week of acclimatization, the mice were randomly divided into five groups (
n
= 16/group): control (no irradiation), 20 Gy (20 Gy single dose), 20 Gy + Fer‐1 (irradiation + ferrostatin‐1, cat. S7243, Selleck Biotechnology Co. Ltd., Houston, Texas, USA), 20 Gy + low‐DHI (irradiation + low‐dose DHI, Z20026866, Shandong Danhong Pharmaceutical Co., Heze, China), and 20 Gy + high‐DHI (irradiation + high‐dose DHI). Localized thoracic irradiation was performed using a small‐animal irradiator (model No. 225, Precision X‐ray Inc., Madison, CT, USA) with shielding to expose only the cardiac region. The mice were monitored for 12 weeks postirradiation, during which four animals in the irradiated groups died. At 2, 4, 8, and 12 weeks postirradiation, the mice were euthanized via intraperitoneal injection of 1% sodium pentobarbital (50 mg/kg). Blood was collected via retro‐orbital puncture, and the hearts were excised, perfused with saline, snap‐frozen in liquid nitrogen, and stored at −80°C. The carcasses were disposed of following institutional biosafety protocols. All procedures were approved by the Ethics Committee of Gansu Provincial Hospital and complied with national animal care guidelines. The experiments were performed under a project license (No. 2024‐464) granted by the ethics board of Gansu Provincial Hospital in compliance with national guidelines for the care and use of animals.
2.2
Serum Biomarker Analysis
Blood samples were allowed to clot at room temperature for 2 h and were then centrifuged at 3000 rpm for 15 min, after which the serum was stored at −80°C. Serum levels of brain natriuretic peptide (BNP, CEA541Mu, cloud‐clone corp., Wuhan, China) and cardiac troponin T (cTnT, SED232Mu, cloud‐clone corp., Wuhan, China) were quantified using enzyme‐linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) kits. Add 100 μL of antibody diluent to each well of the polystyrene microplate and incubate overnight at 4°C. The next day, discard the solution in the well and wash it three times with washing buffer. Add 200 μL of blocking solution to each well and incubate at 37°C for 2 h. Wash it three more times. Add 100 μL of the appropriately diluted sample to be tested to the above‐mentioned coated reaction wells. Seal the plate with sealing film and incubate at 37°C for 2 h. Add 100 μL of the diluted biotinylated antibody working solution to each well. Seal the plate with sealing film and incubate at 37°C for 1 h. Add 100 μL of the diluted enzyme conjugate working solution to each well. Seal the plate with sealing film and incubate at 37°C in the dark for 30 min. Add 100 μL of the substrate solution to each well and react at 37°C in the dark for 30 min until a distinct color gradient appears in the wells of the standard substance diluted in multiple proportions. Add 100 μL of 2 M sulfuric acid to each reaction well, and the color changes from blue to yellow. The absorbance was read at 450 nm using a microplate reader.
Creatine kinase‐MB (CK‐MB), lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), glutathione (GSH), and malondialdehyde (MDA) levels were measured via biochemical assays. After sample loading, perform automatic measurement in a fully automated biochemical analyzer (Chemray 800, Rayto Life and Analytical Sciences Co. Ltd., Shenzhen, China), and then export the data. The data were analyzed and visualized using GraphPad Prism 9.5.
2.3
Histopathological Staining
Myocardial tissues were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde for 24 h, dehydrated, embedded in paraffin, and sectioned (4 μm) using a microtome. For hematoxylin–eosin (H&E) staining, the sections were deparaffinized, rehydrated, and stained with hematoxylin and eosin. For Masson's trichrome staining, the sections were sequentially stained with Weigert's iron hematoxylin, Biebrich scarlet–acid fuchsin, phosphomolybdic acid, and aniline blue to visualize collagen fibers. The sections were imaged under a light microscope.
2.4
Reactive Oxygen Species (
ROS
) Detection via Dihydroethidium (
DHE
) Staining
DHE is a commonly used fluorescent probe for assessing the levels of superoxide anions in tissues and cells. After myocardial tissue was isolated, it was immediately stored in liquid nitrogen. Frozen sections were prepared, and DHE (cat. S0063, Beyotime Biotechnology, Shanghai, China) staining was performed in strict accordance with the instructions for use. Fluorescence is observed under a microscope. ImageJ was used for image analysis.
2.5
Immunohistochemistry (
IHC
)
Paraffin‐embedded sections were subjected to antigen retrieval in citrate buffer (pH 6.0) via microwave heating (95°C, 15 min). Endogenous peroxidase activity was quenched with 3% H
2
O
2
‐methanol. After blocking with 5% BSA, the sections were incubated overnight at 4°C with primary antibodies against glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4, 67763‐1‐Ig, Proteintech Group Inc., Wuhan, China), solute carrier family 7 member 11 (SLC7A11, 26864‐1‐AP, Proteintech Group Inc., Wuhan, China), heme oxygenase 1 (HO‐1, 10701‐1‐AP, Proteintech Group Inc., Wuhan, China), long chain fatty acid coa ligase 4 (ACSL4, 22401‐1‐AP, Proteintech Group Inc., Wuhan, China), and transferrin receptor 1 (TFR1, 65236–1‐IG, Proteintech Group Inc., Wuhan, China). The sections were then incubated with fluorescent secondary antibodies for 1 h at room temperature. DAB substrate was used for chromogenic development, followed by hematoxylin counterstaining. The sections were imaged using a digital pathology scanner.
2.6
Transcriptome Sequencing
Myocardial tissues from the control, 20 Gy, and 20 Gy + DHI groups (
n
= 3 per group) were subjected to transcriptome sequencing. Total ribonucleic acid (RNA) was extracted using TRIzol reagent (cat. 15596018, Invitrogen, Ambion, Carlsbad, CA, USA) and treated with DNase I to remove genomic deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA). mRNA was enriched via oligo (dT) magnetic beads, fragmented, and reverse‐transcribed into cDNA using an NEBNext Ultra II RNA Library Prep Kit. Libraries were size‐selected (250–300 bp) and amplified via PCR. Sequencing was performed on the Illumina NovaSeq 6000 platform to generate 150‐bp paired‐end reads. Raw reads in FASTQ format were processed using fastp (v0.23.2) to remove low‐quality bases (Q < 20) and adapters. Clean reads were aligned to the
Mus musculus
reference genome (GRCm39) using HISAT2 (v2.2.1), and read counts per gene were quantified with HTSeq‐count (v0.13.5). Principal component analysis (PCA) was conducted in R (v4.3.1) to assess intergroup variability. Differential expression genes (DEGs) were identified using DESeq2 (v1.40.2) with thresholds of |log2(fold change) | > 1 and
p
< 0.05. Functional enrichment analyses (Gene Ontology, GO; Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes, KEGG; Reactome) were performed using the clusterProfiler package (v4.10.0) and a hypergeometric test. The raw sequence data reported in this paper have been deposited in the Genome Sequence Archive (Genomics, Proteomics & Bioinformatics 2021) in National Genomics Data Center (Nucleic Acids Res 2022), China National Center for Bioinformation/Beijing Institute of Genomics, Chinese Academy of Sciences (GSA: CRA026320) that are publicly accessible at
https://ngdc.cncb.ac.cn/gsa
.
2.7
Metabolome Sequencing
Myocardial tissues from the control, 20 Gy, and 20 Gy + DHI groups (
n
= 6 per group) were analyzed using liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS, Waters ACQUITY UPLC I‐Class plus, Waters Corporation, Massachusetts, USA) and gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (GC–MS, 8890‐5977B, Agilent Technologies Inc., California, USA).
LC–MS–MS/MS parameters
Ionization: Electrospray ionization (ESI) was performed in positive/negative mode;
Scan mode: Data‐dependent acquisition (DDA);
Chromatography: ACQUITY UPLC BEH C18 column (2.1 × 100 mm, 1.7 μm; Waters); and
Mobile phase: (A) 0.1% formic acid in water; (B) 0.1% formic acid in acetonitrile.
GC–MS parameters
Ionization: Electron impact (EI) at 70 eV;
Temperatures: Ion source (230°C) and quadrupole (150°C);
Scan mode: Full scan (m/z 50–500); and
Column: DB‐5MS capillary column (30 m × 0.25 mm, 0.25 μm; Agilent).
Raw data were preprocessed using Progenesis QI (v3.0, Nonlinear Dynamics) for baseline correction, peak picking, retention time alignment, and normalization. Metabolites were annotated by matching retention times (RTs), exact masses (< 5 ppm error), MS/MS spectra, and isotopic patterns against the Human Metabolome Database (HMDB), LipidMaps (v2.3), METLIN, and LuMet‐Animal database. Differentially abundant metabolites were screened via a combined multivariate (VIP > 1.0 from PLS‐DA) and univariate approach (Student's
t
test,
p
< 0.05). Finally, enrichment analysis of the differentially abundant metabolites was conducted.
2.8
Cell Culture and Irradiation Protocol
The H9C2 and AC16 cell lines were cultured in complete medium consisting of DMEM (Shanghai Yuanpei Biotechnology Co. Ltd., China), 10% fetal bovine serum (ABWbio, Uruguay), and 1% penicillin–streptomycin (100 U/mL penicillin + 100 mg/mL streptomycin; Shanghai Yuanpei Biotechnology). The cells were maintained at 37°C in a humidified incubator with 5% CO
2
and 95% air. The medium was changed every 2–3 days, and the cells were harvested at 80% confluency for experiments.
The experimental groups were as follows: control (no treatment), 8 Gy (single‐dose irradiation), 8 Gy + Fer‐1 (irradiation + Fer‐1), and 8 Gy + DHI (irradiation + DHI). Irradiation was administered using a small‐animal X‐ray irradiator. After irradiation, the culture medium was immediately replenished with fresh medium containing Fer‐1 or DHI, and the cells were cultured for 48 h.
2.9
Cell Viability Assay
Cells were seeded in 96‐well plates (5000 cells/well) and allowed to adhere for 24 h. After irradiation and treatment, 10 μL of cell counting kit‐8 (CCK‐8, cat. M4839, Abmole, Houston, TX, USA) reagent was added to each well, followed by incubation for 2 h. The absorbance at 450 nm was measured using a microplate reader. The data were analyzed with GraphPad Prism 9.5.
2.10
Detection of
LDH
Release in Cells
Cells were cultured for 48 h after modeling, after which the culture supernatant was collected. The instructions of the testing kit (cat. A020‐2‐2, Nanjing Jiancheng Bioengineering Institute, Nanjing, China) were strictly followed. A microplate reader was used to measure the OD value at 450 nm, and GraphPad Prism 9.5 was used for statistical analysis and plotting.
2.11
Oxidative Stress Markers (
GSH
and
MDA
)
After the cells were established, they were cultured for 48 h, digested with trypsin containing EDTA, and resuspended in PBS. To lyse the cells and release intracellular substances, the cells were placed in a −80°C freezer for 10 min and then immersed in a room temperature water bath for 5 min; this process was repeated 3 times. After centrifugation, the supernatant was collected. To assess GSH (cat. S0053, Beyotime Biotechnology, Shanghai, China) and MDA (cat. S0131S, Beyotime Biotechnology, Shanghai, China), the steps described in the user manual were strictly followed. Finally, GraphPad Prism 9.5 was used for statistical analysis and plotting.
2.12
Flow Cytometry
For ROS detection, cells were stained with 10 μM DCFH‐DA (cat. E004‐1‐1, Nanjing Jiancheng Bioengineering Institute) for 30 min at 37°C. To determine the mitochondrial membrane potential (JC‐1, cat. C2003S, Beyotime Biotechnology, Shanghai, China), the cells were incubated with JC‐1 dye in accordance with the manufacturer's instructions. Fluorescence was analyzed using a flow cytometer with FITC/PE channels. The data were processed using FlowJo v10.8.1 and GraphPad Prism 9.5.
2.13
Quantitative Real‐Time
PCR
Total RNA was extracted from H9C2 cells using Trizol (cat. 15596018, Invitrogen, Ambion, Carlsbad, CA, USA) and reverse transcribed into cDNA using the EasyQuick RT MasterMix kit (cat. CW2019M, CWBIO, Taizhou, China). Real‐time PCR was performed using the UltraSYBR Mixture kit (cat. CW0957H, CWBIO, Taizhou, China). Using β‐actin as an internal reference gene, the relative expression of mRNA levels was calculated using the delta–delta Ct method. The primers used in this study are listed in Table
S1
.
2.14
Transmission Electron Microscopy (
TEM
)
After the cells were established, they were cultured for 48 h, digested with trypsin containing EDTA, and fixed with electron microscopy fixative for at least 2 h. Myocardial tissue was immediately soaked in electron microscopy fixative and stored in the dark after isolation. The samples were then fixed in a 1% aqueous solution of osmium tetroxide containing 0.1% potassium ferrocyanide for 1 h. The samples were washed with PBS, dehydrated with a series of graded ethanol solutions, treated overnight with acetone and embedding agent at 37°C, and polymerized at 60°C for 48 h. After preparing ultrasections, the sections were stained with a uranyl acetate and lead citrate solution saturated with 2% ethanol for 15 min and left at room temperature overnight. Finally, images were captured using a TEM (Talos F200C, 200 kV, FEI, Hillsborough, OR, USA) for subsequent analysis.
2.15
Western Blot (
WB
)
Total protein was extracted using RIPA lysis buffer (1 mM PMSF) and quantified via a BCA assay. Proteins were separated by SDS–PAGE and transferred to PVDF membranes. The membranes were blocked with 5% nonfat milk, incubated overnight at 4°C with primary antibodies (1:1000 dilution), and incubated with HRP‐conjugated secondary antibodies (1:3000) for 1 h. Protein bands were visualized using enhanced chemiluminescence (ECL) substrate and quantified with ImageJ.
2.16
Statistical Analysis
The results are expressed as means ± standard deviations (SDs). The comparison between two groups was conducted using a
t
‐test, and one‐way analysis of variance (ANOVA) and two‐way analysis of variance (ANOVA) were used to analyze the statistical significance of multi‐group comparisons. A 95% confidence interval was applied, and a
p
< 0.05 was considered to indicate statistical significance. All the data were analyzed and visualized as bar graphs using GraphPad Prism 9.5.

Introduction
Radiotherapy has significantly improved the survival rates for cancer patients; however, it inevitably leads to complications, among which radiation‐induced heart disease (RIHD) is among the most severe [
1
,
2
]. With the growing population of long‐term cancer survivors, RIHD has emerged as a critical concern, as it negates some therapeutic benefits of radiotherapy and contributes to cardiovascular‐related mortality [
3
,
4
]. Currently, no effective clinical interventions exist for RIHD, underscoring the urgent need to elucidate its pathogenesis and identify novel therapeutic strategies. Accumulating evidence, including findings from our research group, suggests that traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) formulations may offer promising outcomes in the management of RIHD [
5
,
6
].
Our previous studies demonstrated that tanshinone IIA alleviates RIHD by suppressing apoptosis and oxidative stress [
5
,
7
]. Additionally, aloe‐emodin has been reported to mitigate RIHD by inhibiting P4HB lactylation and ameliorating kynurenine metabolic disturbances [
8
]. Danggui Buxue Tang, a classical TCM decoction, improves RIHD via the Nrf2/HMGB1 signaling pathway [
9
]. Danhong injection (DHI), a modern TCM formulation extracted from
Salvia miltiorrhiza
and
Carthamus tinctorius
, is widely used in clinical practice for treating cardiovascular diseases [
10
,
11
]. Preclinical studies indicate that DHI exerts therapeutic effects through antiapoptotic, antioxidant, and anti‐inflammatory mechanisms [
12
].
While oxidative stress is a well‐recognized contributor to RIHD, the role of ferroptosis—a regulated cell death pathway closely linked to oxidative stress—remains underexplored in this context [
13
,
14
]. The aim of this study was to establish in vivo and in vitro RIHD models to delineate the manifestations of ferroptosis in RIHD pathogenesis and evaluate whether DHI exerts therapeutic effects by modulating ferroptosis. Furthermore, transcriptomic and metabolomic sequencing of irradiated murine myocardium was employed to characterize postradiation alterations in gene and metabolite expression profiles.

C2003S, Beyotime Biotechnology, Shanghai, China), the cells were incubated with JC‐1 dye in accordance with the manufacturer's instructions. Fluorescence was analyzed using a flow cytometer with FITC/PE channels. The data were processed using FlowJo v10.8.1 and GraphPad Prism 9.5.
2.13
Quantitative Real‐Time
PCR
Total RNA was extracted from H9C2 cells using Trizol (cat. 15596018, Invitrogen, Ambion, Carlsbad, CA, USA) and reverse transcribed into cDNA using the EasyQuick RT MasterMix kit (cat. CW2019M, CWBIO, Taizhou, China). Real‐time PCR was performed using the UltraSYBR Mixture kit (cat. CW0957H, CWBIO, Taizhou, China). Using β‐actin as an internal reference gene, the relative expression of mRNA levels was calculated using the delta–delta Ct method. The primers used in this study are listed in Table
S1
.
2.14
Transmission Electron Microscopy (
TEM
)
After the cells were established, they were cultured for 48 h, digested with trypsin containing EDTA, and fixed with electron microscopy fixative for at least 2 h. Myocardial tissue was immediately soaked in electron microscopy fixative and stored in the dark after isolation. The samples were then fixed in a 1% aqueous solution of osmium tetroxide containing 0.1% potassium ferrocyanide for 1 h. The samples were washed with PBS, dehydrated with a series of graded ethanol solutions, treated overnight with acetone and embedding agent at 37°C, and polymerized at 60°C for 48 h. After preparing ultrasections, the sections were stained with a uranyl acetate and lead citrate solution saturated with 2% ethanol for 15 min and left at room temperature overnight. Finally, images were captured using a TEM (Talos F200C, 200 kV, FEI, Hillsborough, OR, USA) for subsequent analysis.
2.15
Western Blot (
WB
)
Total protein was extracted using RIPA lysis buffer (1 mM PMSF) and quantified via a BCA assay. Proteins were separated by SDS–PAGE and transferred to PVDF membranes. The membranes were blocked with 5% nonfat milk, incubated overnight at 4°C with primary antibodies (1:1000 dilution), and incubated with HRP‐conjugated secondary antibodies (1:3000) for 1 h. Protein bands were visualized using enhanced chemiluminescence (ECL) substrate and quantified with ImageJ.
2.16
Statistical Analysis
The results are expressed as means ± standard deviations (SDs). The comparison between two groups was conducted using a
t
‐test, and one‐way analysis of variance (ANOVA) and two‐way analysis of variance (ANOVA) were used to analyze the statistical significance of multi‐group comparisons. A 95% confidence interval was applied, and a
p
< 0.05 was considered to indicate statistical significance. All the data were analyzed and visualized as bar graphs using GraphPad Prism 9.5.

4
Discussion
In this study, we investigated, after establishing in vivo and in vitro models, whether DHI exerts therapeutic action against RIHD through antioxidant and antiferroptotic effects. First, on the basis of numerous literature reports and previous results from our research group, X‐rays can induce myocardial tissue and cell damage both in vivo and in vitro. That finding was confirmed in this study. After X‐ray irradiation, tissue dissolution was induced, as determined by HE staining, and the degree of fibrosis increased with prolonged feeding time, as determined by Masson's trichrome staining. Damage indicators, such as BNP, CK‐MB, LDH, AST, and cTnT, were detected in vivo and in vitro (cell activity, LDH). In addition, damage to the microstructure of mitochondria was observed through TEM, and a decrease in the mitochondrial membrane potential was detected by flow cytometry. At present, DHI is widely used to treat cardiovascular diseases. In this study, DHI was administered to mice and myocardial cells, and the RIHD‐related alterations mentioned earlier were reversed, indicating that DHI has a certain degree of therapeutic effect on RIHD.
Ferroptosis is a novel form of cell death characterized by the absence of mitochondrial cristae [
15
,
16
,
17
]. Iron death is caused mainly by ROS, especially when a large amount of lipid peroxides are produced and the permeability of the membrane increases, disrupting ion homeostasis, affecting the normal structure and function of the membrane, and ultimately leading to cell death [
18
]. ACSL4 is considered a key biomarker for ferroptosis. Knocking down ACSL4 can inhibit ferroptosis, while overexpressing ASCL4 can promote sensitivity to ferroptosis by regulating the cellular lipid composition [
19
]. The Xc‐GSH‐GPX4 pathway is the main pathway regulating ferroptosis, and the main mechanism for reducing ROS through this pathway is dependent on the redox ability of GSH. GSH is a tripeptide consisting of glutamic acid, cysteine, and glycine that has antioxidant properties; it is a substrate for GPX4, which can be converted into oxidized glutathione (GSSG) to exert strong antioxidant effects and inhibit ferroptosis [
20
]. In addition, system Xc consists of subunit SLC7A11 and solute carrier family 3 member 2 (SLC3A2), which mediate the exchange of cysteine and glutamate on the plasma membrane at a 1:1 ratio, synthesizing GSH and participating in ferroptosis [
21
]. Iron (Fe
2+
) can react with oxygen or hydrogen peroxide (H
2
O
2
) to produce large amounts of hydroxyl radicals and lipid peroxides, ultimately leading to iron death [
22
]. HO‐1 also participates in iron homeostasis, playing a role in the degradation of heme and the production of ferrous iron. The activation of ferritin autophagy or the overexpression of HO‐1 can increase free iron levels, leading to the accumulation of lipid peroxides and ultimately resulting in iron death [
23
,
24
,
25
]. In addition, TFR1 is located on the surface of the cell membrane and is responsible for binding to transferrin to transport iron ions into cells. TFR1 overexpression enhances iron absorption, leading to an increase in intracellular free iron levels and exacerbating lipid peroxidation [
26
,
27
,
28
].
80% of tissues and cells are composed of water, and irradiation damage is caused mostly by ROS produced by the irradiation decomposition of water, which is an important source of damage to normal tissues after irradiation [
29
]. When intracellular antioxidants cannot fully eliminate ROS, the oxidative/antioxidant balance is disrupted, leading to oxidative stress [
30
,
31
]. In this study, TEM revealed that the integrity of the mitochondria was damaged and the continuity of the mitochondrial cristae was poor in myocardial tissue and cells irradiated with X‐rays. DHE staining and flow cytometry revealed increases in ROS levels, decreases in GSH levels, increases in MDA levels, and decreases in the mitochondrial membrane potential. In addition, the expression of GPX4 and SLC7A11, which are associated with ferroptosis, decreased, whereas the expression of HO‐1, ACSL4, and TFR1 increased. These data suggest that X‐rays can induce ferroptosis in the heart. The antioxidant capacity of DHI has been demonstrated in numerous studies. When we treated experimental animals and in vitro‐generated cells with DHI, we found that mitochondrial integrity was restored and that JC‐1 was elevated. Moreover, the GSH content increased, and the MDA content decreased. GPX4 and SLC7A11 expression increased, whereas HO‐1, ACSL4, and TFR1 expression decreased. These results indicate that DHI serves as an antioxidant and has a potential inhibitory effect on ferroptosis.
Through individual transcriptome or metabolome analysis, we found that DEGs or differentially abundant metabolites were enriched mainly in immune system‐related biological processes or pathways when comparing the irradiation and control groups. When comparing the drug and irradiation groups, in addition to immune system‐related biological processes, various metabolic processes and signaling pathways were involved. Second, through a joint omics analysis, we identified many valuable RNA–metabolite combinations. These results provide a good basis for future research and target screening by our research group.
5
Conclusion
In summary, the results of this study indicate that DHI exerts therapeutic effects against RIHD by inhibiting ferroptosis. Furthermore, the results of transcriptome and metabolome analyses provide targets and research directions for studies on RIHD from different perspectives.
